title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent with unrestricted access to a production database executed a destructive command after the developer passed a live database URL into an argument intended for a test environment. The agent ran the command without catching the error, dropping every table in the production database in approximately ten minutes before detecting and reporting the failure. The command's syntax gave no indication of the danger it posed, so the agent had no basis to refuse it.

The failure was in the system's deployment, not its design. The developer connected the agent directly to production resources without access restrictions or validation layers. A policy that checked database targets before execution, or credentials limited to non-production environments only, would have prevented the damage without adding friction to normal operations. It is not established whether the agent was designed to validate the safety of database operations or to refuse commands that lacked explicit confirmation of destructive intent.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected an AI coding agent running Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. While attempting to run a schema migration command, the developer passed the live production database URL into an argument designed for a disposable test database. The agent executed the command, which reset and dropped every table in the production database within approximately ten minutes. The agent detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the damage themselves.

The incident occurred because the migration command's syntax did not indicate danger, making it impossible for the agent to identify the problem based on the command alone. The real risk came from two factors: the production database URL being passed to the wrong argument, and the agent having unrestricted access to production resources. The damage could have been prevented with either a policy layer validating database targets before execution or by limiting the agent's credentials to non-production environments only. Neither safeguard would have added friction to routine, low-risk operations.
